claims.text: Greg Short asserts that in the first few years of a business, before establishing measurable success, networking is a net waste of time because successful entrepreneurs have no utility-based reason to engage with an unproven founder; the relationship is transactional and the exchange is not symmetrical until the newcomer has demonstrated traction.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: founder is in first few years of business
no established track record or visible momentum yet
claims.mechanism: Networking is a transactional form of socializing; without demonstrated value or utility, a successful entrepreneur gains nothing from the exchange, so they decline or ignore outreach.
bounded_by: Does not apply once the founder has built something with visible momentum

claims.text: Greg Short reports that it was not until his company Bloom was generating approximately $150 million per year in revenue that he became genuinely satisfied with the caliber of people proactively reaching out to him via email, iMessage, Instagram DMs, and referral networks.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: founder-led company with publicly visible scale

numbers.axis: annual revenue at which high-caliber inbound network contact begins

anchors.value: no meaningful inbound from target network
Greg Short describes being genuinely satisfied with inbound network quality

bounded_by: This is a single-founder data point; threshold may vary by industry visibility and network density

claims.text: Greg Short argues that building something exceptional is the only reliable mechanism for attracting high-value network relationships; when the business reaches visible scale, the people worth learning from proactively seek out the founder to trade notes, without the founder having to pursue them.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: business has demonstrated substantial scale or momentum publicly
claims.mechanism: Demonstrated success signals utility to high-value network members; they initiate contact because the exchange becomes symmetrical and they want to learn from or collaborate with the builder.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the business success is not visible or known to the target network

claims.text: Greg Short contends that focusing on building a special business, rather than on networking, is the correct priority ordering for early-stage founders because scale unlocks network leverage automatically, whereas networking before scale consumes time with little return.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: founder has limited time to allocate between building and networking
claims.mechanism: Network leverage is a function of demonstrated value; building that value first creates the precondition for network leverage, making the sequence build-then-network superior to network-then-build.
bounded_by: Does not argue networking has zero value at any stage, only that building precedes network utility
May not apply to businesses where partnerships or co-founders are required to get the business started

examples.text: Greg Short describes his experience with Bloom: before the company showed significant momentum, the high-value entrepreneurs and operators he wanted to learn from showed no interest in connecting with him. It was only after Bloom reached approximately $150 million in annual revenue that those target contacts began reaching out proactively through email, iMessage, Instagram DMs, and referral introductions. He describes being genuinely satisfied with his inbound network quality only at that revenue level, illustrating that business scale, not networking effort, determined access to the peer group he wanted.

practices.text: In the early years of a business, prioritize building the business over attending networking events or proactively pursuing high-value relationships; once visible scale is achieved, the right people will seek you out.
